title: Media consumption is reorganizing around persistent fandom, fragmented platforms, creator connection, and AI-enabled continuity between releases
source_unit: Deloitte Center for Technology, Media & Telecommunications, 2026 Digital Media Trends: Capturing always-on fandom between releases and seasons, 25 March 2026
geography: United States consumer media and entertainment behavior across streaming, social media, music, gaming, live events, creators, and fandom communities

observations.period: 2025-2026; US media consumption and subscription context

denominator.unit: US consumers age 14 and older surveyed online in October-November 2025, weighted to the Census

media_time.unit: hours per day spent on media and entertainment activities by the average consumer

svod_households.unit: percent of US households with a paid subscription video-on-demand service; subscribing households average four services

svod_churn.unit: percent of consumers who cancelled an SVOD service in the last six months

return_churn.unit: percent of consumers who churned and returned to the same SVOD service in the last six months

analytic_route.value: more choice and subscription fragmentation are pushing media companies toward retention, cross-format engagement, and deeper fan relationships

observations.method: Deloitte Digital Media Trends online survey of 3,575 US consumers, supplemented by longitudinal media and entertainment analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Subscription and churn measures are survey-based and period-specific; they do not establish household-level expenditure causes, platform profitability, or whether a given retention strategy works.
observations.subgroup: US media consumers, SVOD households, streamers, social-video users, music and gaming audiences, content providers, advertisers, and creators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Subscription churn can reflect seasonal timing, price changes, content availability, or household sharing; fragmentation may coexist with stable total media time.

observations.period: 2025-2026; fandom as a cross-platform consumer segment

denominator.unit: US consumers surveyed; fan status is self-identification with at least one entertainment or cultural category

fan_prevalence.unit: approximate percent of consumers who identify as fans of at least one entertainment category

fan_media_time.unit: additional minutes of daily media and entertainment time for fans relative to nonfans, approximately 16 percent more

fan_svod.value: 92 percent of fans versus 77 percent of nonfans use SVOD; subscribing fans spend $71 per month across an average of four services versus $56 across three services for nonfans

cross_platform_fandom.unit: percent of fans who say being a fan often leads them to engage across multiple platforms, rising to about 70% among Gen Z and millennial fans

analytic_route.value: fandom behaves as a continuous, multichannel relationship rather than a release-date event

observations.method: Weighted Deloitte survey with self-identified fan segmentation across music, film and TV, sports, gaming, creators, genres, brands, and hobbies.
observations.uncertainty: The fan definition is self-selected and differs from earlier Deloitte reports; higher spending and time among fans are descriptive associations, not causal effects of fandom.
observations.subgroup: Fans and nonfans, Gen Z, millennials, older generations, creators, franchise owners, streamers, music and gaming services, and live-event providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fans may be more likely to have high media engagement before identifying as fans; cross-platform activity may increase exposure without translating into durable loyalty or value.

denominator.unit: US consumers surveyed, with fan and generational subgroup comparisons

social_relevance.unit: percent of consumers who say social media content is more relevant to them than traditional media content

creator_connection.unit: percent of consumers who feel a stronger personal connection to social media creators than to TV personalities or actors

fan_discovery.unit: percent of fans who say social media is their primary way to discover new content, rising to 73% among Gen Z fans

off_platform_path.unit: percent of fans who discover content on social media and then go elsewhere to watch, listen to, or buy the full version; the share approaches 60% among Gen Z fans

attention_route.value: social platforms and creator communities increasingly mediate discovery while monetization and behavioral visibility may remain split across platforms

observations.method: Deloitte survey comparisons among all consumers, fans, and generational fan groups, with analysis of the discovery-to-consumption path.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are stated preferences and self-reports; they do not quantify attribution, conversion, creator income, or the distributional effects of platform algorithms.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z fans, older fans, creators, social-video platforms, studios, streamers, advertisers, and audiences moving between social and owned media environments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social discovery can complement rather than displace traditional media, and reported personal connection need not imply trust, civic influence, or long-term creator loyalty.

observations.period: 2025-2026; generative AI and always-on fan engagement

denominator.unit: US consumers surveyed, including self-identified fans

labeled_ai_content.unit: approximate percent of fans who would accept AI-created content on SVOD, social media, music services, and video games if clearly labeled

personalized_digest.unit: approximate percent of fans interested in AI-created personalized digests of streaming, social, podcast, and actor updates

sports_highlights.unit: percent of sports fans interested in personalized highlight reels and commentary based on favorite teams and athletes

cocreation.unit: approximate percent of fans interested in cocreating content with generative AI, such as alternative endings

infrastructure_route.value: generative AI is framed as connective infrastructure for recommendations, summaries, cross-platform identity, and year-round fan engagement

observations.method: Deloitte survey of US consumers and fans, combined with strategic analysis of generative-AI applications in media and entertainment.
observations.uncertainty: Interest in labeled AI content is not adoption or willingness to pay; the report does not resolve copyright, labor, privacy, authenticity, or recommendation-quality risks.
observations.subgroup: Fans, sports fans, Gen Z and millennial audiences, media companies, rights holders, creators, advertisers, AI providers, and platform operators.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI-generated summaries and personalized content may increase convenience while weakening provenance, creator control, cultural serendipity, or human editorial judgment.

related_sources.claim: Deloitte's Digital Media Monitor provides longitudinal subscription, churn, social-video, and consumer-media measures.
Deloitte's 2026 Media and Entertainment Industry Outlook provides complementary industry and AI-generated-content context.

boundary: This record adds a Deloitte consumer-media signal about fandom, streaming fragmentation, creator-mediated discovery, and labeled generative-AI engagement. It is aggregate survey and industry analysis, not respondent-level ingestion, a causal panel, a global cultural census, a measure of creator welfare, or proof that platform aggregation benefits audiences.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Deloitte Digital Media Trends 2026 page reviewed for survey size and weighting, media and subscription metrics, fan segmentation, cross-platform discovery, creator connection, and generative-AI interest measures.
